description: Equipo ambicioso, compuesto por estudiantes y profesionales de ingeniería y biotecnología, apasionados por los desafíos de innovación. Nuestra fuerza reside en combinar rigor científico, datos precisos y una sólida experiencia humana para diseñar soluciones disruptivas. Destacamos en análisis de datos, diseño 3D, integración de IoT, microbiología, soft skills de comunicación y trabajo colaborativo, que potencian la sinergia y la creatividad del equipo. ¡Desde San Luis hacia todo el universo!
summary:
When a crew travels beyond Earth's orbit, latencies of up to 22 minutes each way make real-time telemedicine impossible—the crew must become its own clinical team.

AURORA (Autonomous Resilience & Health Copilot) is an offline (edge computing) operational health and psychological resilience ecosystem mitigating NASA’s 5 spaceflight hazards. Built on Quiet UX and salutogenic theory, it integrates NASA's Spaceflight Standard Measures—Cognition battery, neuro-ocular (SANS), carotid thickness (CIMT), bone density, and HRV—via a conversational copilot that turns biomedical data into preventive self-regulation.

Key capabilities:
* Asymmetric Alerts & Privacy: Guides astronauts with non-alarmist micro-actions to prevent biomarker anxiety, discreetly alerting the Crew Medical Officer or crew only during critical risks.
* 4-Environment Adaptability: Environment-Aware UI across habitat consoles (1920x1080), haptic smartwatches, and minimalist helmet HUDs for Transit, Orbital Stations, Rover/EVA, and Planetary Surfaces.
* Circadian & Countermeasures: Combats monotony via a longitudinal calendar, exercise tracking (ARED/treadmill/cycle), cognitive mini-games, and Earth-scenery exergaming.
* Mental Health (Quiet Space): Combines 3D Audio biophilic soundscapes, automated CBT guides, and an encrypted micro-venting journal generating anonymized crew climate reports.

Impact: AURORA ensures crew cohesion, cognitive agility, and medical self-sufficiency for Artemis and Mars missions.
details:
AURORA: Integrated Operational Health System for Deep Space Missions

1. Abstract

Long-duration space exploration missions to the Moon and Mars mark a critical transition from Low Earth Orbit (LEO) operations. The astronomical distances involved introduce round-trip communication delays of up to twenty-two minutes each way with Earth, making real-time medical and telepsychological assistance from Mission Control impossible. Furthermore, the five hazards identified by NASA's Human Research Program (HRP)—space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, variable gravity fields, and hostile or closed environments—interact synergistically. This interaction primarily escalates the risks of cognitive impairment, circadian disruption, space asthenia, and loss of crew cohesion.

In this context, we present  AURORA (Autonomous Resilience & Health Copilot ), an integrated software system for operational health and psycho-emotional well-being engineered to assist spaceflight crews. AURORA combines a high-resolution visual interface for desktop displays (1920x1080, 16:9) with a mobile wearable ecosystem that processes real-time signals from spacesuits, wearable sensors, and on-board medical diagnostic devices (such as portable ultrasound scanners and lab-on-a-chip blood/urine analyzers). The system architecture is built around three core pillars: a Quiet UX paradigm (a silent, non-alarmist user experience), an anthropomorphic conversational copilot acting as a clinical-affective assistant, and an intelligent asymmetric notification protocol that protects astronaut privacy while discreetly alerting the Crew Medical Officer (CMO) and crew regarding operational risks. By incorporating NASA Spaceflight Standard Measures—such as the  Cognition  test battery, carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) vascular ultrasound monitoring, SANS neuro-ocular evaluation, and rest-activity actigraphy—AURORA transforms biomedical monitoring into a salutogenic, preventive, and context-aware process adapted to diverse mission environments (IVA, EVA, and planetary surface exploration).

Keywords:  Space Health, Bioastronautics, Psychological Resilience, Cognitive Ergonomics, Quiet UX, Crew Autonomy, NASA Spaceflight Standard Measures, Interplanetary Missions.

2. Introduction

The expansion of human presence into deep space through the Artemis program and future crewed missions to Mars represents a fundamental paradigm shift in bioastronautics. Unlike operations aboard the International Space Station (ISS), where emergency medical evacuation or real-time psychiatric teleconsultation remains feasible, interplanetary missions demand an unprecedented level of medical and psychological self-sufficiency. During periods of extreme physiological stress, subtle hypoxia, or accumulated fatigue, interpreting raw biomedical data—such as complex electrocardiographic waveforms, rapid blood volume shifts, or ionizing radiation dosimetry in sieverts—imposes a dangerous cognitive load on crew members. AURORA resolves this operational bottleneck by functioning as an intelligent translation layer between raw physiological telemetric data and clinical-operational decision-making.

NASA's Human Research Program (HRP) synthesizes the threats facing astronauts into five fundamental hazards:

  • Space radiation:  cumulative exposure to Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR) and Solar Particle Events (SPE), which induce neuroinflammation, hippocampal structural alterations, and heightened long-term oncological and cardiovascular risks.
  • Isolation and confinement:  extended stays within constrained habitats and mandatory interaction within small groups for months or years, fostering interpersonal friction, sensory deprivation/fatigue, and affective mood disorders.
  • Distance from Earth:  psychological isolation exacerbated by the loss of direct visual contact with Earth ("Earth-out-of-view phenomenon") alongside severe telemetry and telecommunication propagation delays.
  • Variable gravity fields:  physiological adaptations resulting from prolonged microgravity exposure and transitions to partial gravity environments, inducing cephalad fluid shifts, cardiovascular deconditioning, progressive loss of bone mineral density, and skeletal muscle atrophy.
  • Hostile and confined environments:  internal habitat environmental stressors—including continuous acoustic background noise, elevated partial pressure of ambient carbon dioxide, desynchronizing artificial lighting spectrums, and altered microbial ecology—can alter the immune system and increase the susceptibility to hypersensitivities and infectious pathogens.

Traditional hospital information systems and clinical telemetry software are unviable in deep space due to their intrusive and alarmist design. Conventional systems trigger "biomarker anxiety" and foster technology avoidance among crew members. AURORA mitigates these risks through a digital environment centered on user psychology, guided self-regulation, and operational performance preservation. The platform enables astronauts to autonomously evaluate their health status, identify unfavorable parameter trends, execute preventive countermeasures, and manage emergent clinical scenarios effectively.

3. Theoretical and Clinical Rationale

3.1. Cognitive and Psychosocial Vulnerabilities in Long-Duration Spaceflight

Evidence reports from NASA's Behavioral Health and Performance (BHP) Element and peer-reviewed bioastronautics literature indicate that while acute, severe psychiatric disorders have historically been rare in spaceflight, the incidence of asthenic symptoms, emotional lability, irritability, and declines in cognitive processing speed scales exponentially with mission duration. Empirical studies demonstrate statistically significant decrements in cognitive processing speed, visual working memory, and sustained attention during early flight phases. These subtle impairments create critical operational vulnerability windows, compromising mission objectives and crew safety during complex maneuvers.

3.2. Design Philosophy: quiet UX and salutogenesis

Standard clinical monitoring systems flag physiological anomalies using flashing red alerts and high-decibel auditory alarms. In an astronaut already experiencing hypervigilance within a high-hazard environment, these intrusive notifications trigger acute activation of the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) axis, elevating systemic cortisol levels and compounding cardiovascular and autonomic strain.

AURORA operationalizes Salutogenic Theory (Antonovsky), focusing on bolstering factors that cultivate health, physiological equilibrium, and psychological resilience (sense of coherence) rather than focusing exclusively on pathogenesis. The interface architecture adheres strictly to the Quiet UX  paradigm:

  • Cognitive Ergonomics & Hick's Law: visual clutter is systematically eliminated. The software restricts screen views to essential parameters tailored to the active operational environment, minimizing decision time during states of mental fatigue.
  • Biophilic Color Perception: high-contrast sci-fi neon aesthetics are replaced with biophilic color palettes derived from terrestrial environments (moss greens, warm slate grays, soft sand tones). This visual environment promotes cortical alpha wave synchronization and relaxation.
  • Non-Punitive Cognitive Reframing: physiological deviations are never displayed as "failures" or "diseases." Instead, they are framed as temporary physiological demand states requiring self-regulation countermeasures (e.g., micro-pauses, heart rate variability coherence training, sensory immersion).

4. AURORA System Development

4.1. Functional Capabilities and Operational Architecture

Biomedical telemetric data is aggregated into a central  Mission Control (Fig. 1) dashboard and individual crew profiles (Fig 2.). Measurements are continuously benchmarked against personalized astronaut baselines, enabling multivariate analysis, automated anomaly detection, sensor signal loss diagnostics, and a tiered criticality alerting system equipped with Emergency Override protocols and AI-assisted clinical guidance.

Figure 1. Mission Control.

Figure 2. Body schema and individual indicators. 

To maintain operational integrity in deep space, AURORA operates entirely offline using edge-computing architecture. It requires zero terrestrial server connectivity, ensuring seamless continuity during signal blackouts and maintaining persistent onboard historical data storage. Its multi-device interface adapts dynamically across operational contexts—presenting minimal HUD overlays for helmet visors, habitat ambient displays, and detailed clinical diagnostic suites (Fig. 3). System features include comprehensive crew management, role-based access control (RBAC), full audit logging, data export capabilities, multi-language support, adaptive light/dark visual modes, and an integration API.

Figure 3. Visor view.

4.2. Multilayer Architecture and Environmental Adaptability

AURORA is structured as a modular software platform running fully locally onboard (offline edge computing). The system operates across three interconnected interface layers:

  1. Main Desktop Workstation (1920x1080 - 16:9):  designed for fixed displays within habitat modules, featuring a wide panoramic layout anchored by a fixed Left Vertical Sidebar to optimize clinical and operational workflows.
  2. Companion Wearable Device (Smartwatch):  a tactile smartwatch utilizing subtle haptic feedback to accompany astronauts during daily routines. It continuously gathers passive physiological metrics (HRV, circadian actigraphy, pulse oximetry) and emits gentle vibrational prompts for guided breathing exercises or hydration reminders without disrupting active tasks.
  3. Minimalist Aerospace Helmet HUD Display:  streamlined visual overlays integrated into spacesuit helmet viewports, displaying real-time asymmetric alerts and critical environmental parameters during Extravehicular Activity (EVA).
The parameters selected for monitoring are as follows, as shown in Figure 4:
  • Heart Rate and Heart Rate Variability (HRV): cardiovascular stability, autonomic tone, physiological stress, and fatigue.
  • Oxygen Saturation (SpO₂): blood oxygen supply, oxygenation issues, and hypoxemia.
  • Core and Peripheral Body Temperature: identification of thermal abnormalities such as hyperthermia or hypothermia.
  • Radiation Exposure (Current/Cumulative Rate): monitoring of space radiation.
  • Solar Particle Event (SPE) Alert: real-time dosage monitoring during solar storms in deep space.
  • Body Fluid Redistribution and Balance, and Intraocular Pressure (IOP): cephalad fluid shift, jugular vein diameter/flow, hydration levels, and intraocular pressure to prevent SANS (Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome).
  • Psychosocial Stress and Mood Index: mental health assessment via voice analysis and micro-check-ins during periods of prolonged confinement.
  • Sleep Architecture and Circadian Rhythm: prevention of circadian desynchronization during long-duration travel.
  • Countermeasure Compliance (ARED/Treadmill/Cycle): tracking of mechanical load and intensity to mitigate the loss of bone and muscle density.
  • Cabin/Habitat Atmosphere and Air Quality: environmental control of CO2, O2, humidity, cabin pressure, and ambient noise to prevent hypercapnia and headaches in enclosed environments.
  • Plasma Volume and Vascular Tone: monitoring of cardiovascular deconditioning.
  • Cognitive Performance/Reaction Time: assessment prior to critical tasks such as docking or maintenance.
  • Suit/Rover Pressure and CO2: vital parameters for pressurization and the composition of breathable gas mixtures.
  • Real-Time Metabolic Rate and Caloric Expenditure: monitoring of physical exhaustion and thermal regulation within the suit.
  • Hydration and Life Support Consumables: remaining capacity of cooling water, batteries, and oxygen.
  • Respiratory Rate and Core Temperature: detection of respiratory distress or overheating resulting from strenuous physical activity.
  • Musculoskeletal Load in Partial Gravity: muscle adaptation and the response of weight-bearing bones following transit through microgravity.
  • Habitat Air Quality (Regolith/Dust Particles): monitoring of respiratory contaminants introduced from the surface.
  • Gait Biomechanics and Neuromuscular Fatigue: postural stability to prevent falls on uneven terrain.
  • Surface Dosimetry: radiation exposure based on the local atmosphere or magnetosphere.
  • Neurological and Cognitive Checks: prevention of human error and performance degradation prior to critical maneuvers.
  • Biochemical and Hormonal Health Panel: proactive identification of metabolic, infectious, or hormonal imbalances.
  • Long-Term Bone and Muscle Health: monitoring of cumulative physical wear to prevent serious injuries upon returning to a gravity environment.

Figure 4. Stored trends and comparison.

The system incorporates an Environment-Aware UI that dynamically adapts the information displayed on the main screen based on the astronaut’s environment and the mission context. Accordingly, parameters have been classified into two categories: vital parameters, which must remain fixed in the main view, and environment-specific parameters.

Vital parameters:

  • Heart Rate (HR) and Heart Rate Variability (HRV: RMSSD / SDNN).
  • Peripheral Oxygen Saturation (SpO2).
  • Core and Peripheral Body Temperature.
  • Ionizing Radiation Exposure (Instantaneous Rate and Cumulative Dose).

Parameters by Environment:

The system's Environment-Aware UI dynamically reconfigures display layouts and highlighted parameters based on the active mission phase, as detailed in Table 1:

Table 1. Operational environments, clinical focus areas, and contextual monitoring parameters.

4.3. Assistive Conversational Agent (AURORA Avatar)

To mitigate alienation risks and provide an empathetic Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) channel, the system integrates  AURORA , a virtual conversational copilot supporting voice and text inputs (Fig 5).

Figure 5. Personal user and virtual copilot

To prevent the  Uncanny Valley  effect (the psychological repulsion triggered by imperfect hyperrealistic human representations), the avatar is designed as a stylized, clean entity with smooth geometric contours and serene facial expressions suited for a rigorous professional environment. AURORA avoids infantile language and exaggerated praise, operating as a calm, confidential, and expert copilot that translates complex biomedical metrics into actionable daily operational recommendations.

Accessible via the main Home interface alongside a dedicated dialogue console (Talk to AURORA), the avatar processes natural language commands such as: "Aurora, log my exercise session for today", "What is my HRV recovery trend over the last 72 hours?", or  "Initiate a 4-minute heart rate coherence breathing routine."

4.4. Intelligent Asymmetric Notification Protocol

One of the major breakthroughs in the conception of AURORA is the resolution of the dilemma between individual privacy and the collective safety of the spacecraft. To prevent the astronaut from perceiving the system as a surveillance tool used by Mission Control or their fellow crew members, AURORA implements an Asymmetric Alert Architecture:

  • Individual Level (Affected Crew Member): when an astronaut's telemetry indicates unfavorable physiological fluctuations (e.g., a sharp decrease in HRV accompanied by elevated sympathetic tone or degraded sleep efficiency), the interface  never displays alarmist warning messages. Instead, AURORA delivers a calm, non-punitive prompt:  "Your system registers sustained physical load. A 5-minute biophilic break is recommended prior to your next work module."
  • Crew/Crew Medical Officer (CMO) Level: if a parameter breach crosses a critical clinical threshold that threatens maneuver safety or indicates an incapacitating event (e.g., severe cardiac dysrhythmia, acute EVA spatial disorientation, or unresponsiveness), AURORA routes a discrete notification to the CMO console and crew communications.

This dual-tier approach protects individual crew members from unnecessary anxiety while ensuring timely activation of clinical and operational support networks.

4.5. Functional Breakdown of Key Modules1. Home (Wellness Orbit & Aurora Console)

The primary landing view is centered on the  Resilience Sphere , a fluid visual component pulsing at an optimal respiratory frequency of 6 cycles per minute. Its color gradient evolves smoothly to reflect circadian recovery status (soft blue in the morning, moss green during optimal states, warm amber during elevated fatigue).

The sphere is flanked by the AURORA conversational panel and passive telemetry summary cards covering sleep duration, HRV metrics (RMSSD/SDNN), and a one-tap affective self-assessment (Energized, Stable, Monotonous, Exhausted).

2. Body & Biomarkers (Anatomical Vector Model & NASA Standard Measures)

Featuring an interactive anatomical vector model of the human body, this module aligns directly with NASA Spaceflight Standard Measures. Selecting specific anatomical regions displays target diagnostic indicators:

  • Central Nervous System & Brain: results from the NASA  Cognition  battery—including Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) sustained attention, Fractured 2-Back (F2B) working memory, and Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST) processing speed—alongside non-invasive intracranial pressure estimations.
  • Neuro-Ocular System: spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) risk metrics, optic disc edema monitoring, and intraocular pressure (IOP) tracking.
  • Carotid Vascular System: high-frequency ultrasound Carotid Intima-Media Thickness (CIMT) measurements to assess arterial stiffness and radiation-induced accelerated vascular aging.
  • Cardiovascular System: HRV spectrum analysis, clinical blood pressure trends, and cardiovascular adaptation to cephalad fluid shifts.
  • Musculoskeletal System: relative muscle volume and Bone Mineral Density (BMD) tracking, monitoring microgravity bone degradation rates (1 to 1,5%  monthly density loss).
  • Immunological biomarkers and microbiome: salivary cortisol dynamics, leukocyte/lymphocyte ratios, latent viral reactivation markers, and gut microbiota integrity assessment

Biomedical metrics are displayed using a salutogenic status system: green (optimal), amber (self-regulation required), and red (clinical threshold exceeded).

3. Routine & Calendar (Circadian Alignment & Longitudinal Tracking)

To combat temporal desynchronization in deep space—where terrestrial 24-hour diurnal light cycles are absent—this module features an interactive visual timeline:

  • Critical Habit Compliance: automated tracking of physical exercise duration, daily hydration volume, and sleep-rest schedules.
  • Longitudinal Mission Phases: filters and compares physiological parameters across mission phases ( Pre-flight, In-flight L+30, L-30, Post-flight R+10 ), generating long-term trend lines to detect cumulative degradation.
4. Challenges (Gamification, Exergaming, and Cognitive Agility)

Designed to counteract environmental monotony and sensory deprivation, this module incorporates healthy gamification mechanics:

  • Spatial Exergaming: transforms treadmill and cycle ergometer countermeasure sessions into immersive virtual routes through Earth landscapes (e.g., Patagonian trails, Andean forest paths).
  • Neuro-Cognitive Minigames: rapid 2-minute cognitive challenges engineered to maintain neuroplasticity and executive function.
  • Habit Streaks: visual progress indicators celebrating consistency in self-care routines.
5. Quiet Space (Mental Health & Asynchronous Micro-Venting)

A private self-regulation sanctuary built with enhanced data security:

  • Asynchronous Micro-Venting: enables crew members to record audio notes or write personal journals. Entries are encrypted and stored locally, offering an emotional catharsis channel free from performance evaluation concerns. Aggregate anonymized data allows the system to analyze crew-wide emotional trends.
  • Immersive Biophilic Audio: plays 3D binaural Earth soundscapes (terrestrial rain, ocean waves, forest winds) to restore cognitive capacity diminished by continuous mechanical habitat noise.
  • Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Tools (Automated CBT): interactive Cognitive Behavioral Therapy modules providing interpersonal conflict resolution protocols, diaphragmatic breathing guides, and heart rate coherence exercises.

5. Conclusion

By shifting the paradigm of space biomedical monitoring from intrusive, alarmist telemetry toward an autonomous, salutogenic, and crew-centered operational health system, AURORA directly resolves the critical challenges posed by communication latency and extreme isolation in deep space.

The combination of an Environment-Aware UI adapting across four operational contexts, a non-invasive conversational copilot, passive wearable telemetry, and an asymmetric notification architecture ensures astronaut privacy and autonomy while maintaining mission safety. AURORA protects both the physiological integrity and psychological resilience of spaceflight crews in the extreme environments of deep space, sustaining their functional and emotional connection to Earth. The most important technology in a mission is still the ones who make it possible
